passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel anti-inflammatory compound on cytokine production in cultured human macrophages. Macrophages were isolated from peripheral blood mononuclear cells of 20 healthy volunteers and divided into four experimental groups: (1) untreated control, (2) vehicle-treated, (3) low-dose compound (10 µM), and (4) high-dose compound (50 µM). Cells were stimulated with lipopolysaccharide (LPS) for 24 h, after which supernatants were collected and analyzed for tumor necrosis factor‑α (TNF‑α) and interleukin‑6 (IL‑6) concentrations using ELISA. The study aimed to determine dose‑dependent suppression of pro‑inflammatory cytokines and to assess whether the compound’s effect differed from the vehicle. Data were expressed as mean ± SD, with n = 5 per group. The investigators also measured cell viability via MTT assay to ensure observed cytokine changes were not due to cytotoxicity. Results suggested a significant reduction in TNF‑α and IL‑6 at 50 µM, while 10 µM showed a modest, non‑significant trend. The findings support further investigation of the compound as a potential therapeutic for inflammatory disorders.
stem: Which of the following best describes the primary outcome of the study?

options.A: Reduction in cell viability at high dose
options.B: Dose‑dependent decrease in TNF‑α and IL‑6 levels
options.C: No significant change in cytokine production

explanation: The study’s main finding was a significant, dose‑dependent suppression of TNF‑α and IL‑6 at 50 µM, with a modest trend at 10 µM, indicating the compound’s anti‑inflammatory effect.
trap: Students may confuse the vehicle control with the compound; the vehicle showed no significant cytokine change, highlighting that the effect is due to the compound.

stem: Which experimental design element best controls for the effect of the solvent used to deliver the compound?

options.B: Using a higher dose of the compound

explanation: A vehicle-treated group controls for any effects of the solvent or delivery method, ensuring that observed changes are attributable to the compound itself.
trap: Students may think measuring cell viability controls for solvent effects; viability assesses cytotoxicity, not solvent influence.

stem: Which of the following statements is NOT supported by the data?

options.A: Mean TNF-α in the vehicle group (118.9 pg/mL) was close to that of the untreated control (120.5 pg/mL).
options.B: The 10 µM dose lowered mean TNF-α by about 7% relative to control.
options.C: The high-dose reduction in cytokines proves the compound is safe.
options.D: Mean cell viability was above 95% in every group.

explanation: Correct: C) Cytokine suppression says nothing about overall safety, and mean viability was slightly lower at 50 µM (95.2%). Why the others are wrong: A) 118.9 and 120.5 are close. B) (120.5 - 112.3)/120.5 = 6.8%. D) The viabilities were 98.7, 97.9, 96.5 and 95.2%.
trap: Treating lower cytokine levels as proof of safety; cytokine suppression does not measure toxicity.

stem: Which observation in the table best supports the conclusion that the cytokine reduction at 50 µM was not simply caused by cell death?

options.A: Cell viability remained about 95% at 50 µM, close to the 98.7% of untreated cells.
options.B: TNF-α at 50 µM (65.4 pg/mL) was lower than in untreated cells (120.5 pg/mL).
options.C: IL-6 at 50 µM (45.2 pg/mL) was lower than at 10 µM (80.1 pg/mL).
options.D: TNF-α in the vehicle group (118.9 pg/mL) was close to that of the control group (120.5 pg/mL).

explanation: Correct: A) The MTT viability stayed near 95%, so most cells were alive and cell death cannot explain the large cytokine fall. Why the others are wrong: B) This shows cytokines fell but not whether cells survived. C) This shows a dose relationship, not viability. D) This addresses solvent effects, not cell death.
trap: Picking an observation that shows cytokines fell (B or C) instead of the viability data that address the cell-death alternative.
